slides: Open by making rank the organizing measurement of the chapter. Submersions, immersions, embeddings, local diffeomorphisms, and covering maps are not separate vocabulary islands; they are different ways the derivative controls local dimension, topology, and coordinate normal forms.

Use the route slide to give students a map before the definitions arrive. The lecture moves from proof dependencies to rank fields, constant-rank normal forms, local inverse checks, immersion versus embedding examples, submersion level sets, covering maps, and a parameter lab where rank failure appears and disappears.

The proof graph should be read as the chapter's dependency structure. Rank, injectivity, surjectivity, and local coordinate models feed the main classification statements. The artifact confirms eighteen nodes, sixteen edges, and no directed cycles, so later concepts have a visible proof pathway.

This slide turns rank into data rather than a word in a definition. The fold map changes rank across the critical axis, the cusp loses immersion at the origin, the parabola stays immersed on sampled points, and the projection is a model submersion.

The constant-rank theorem is the chapter's local normal-form machine. In suitable coordinates, a rank r map is just the first r coordinates followed by zeros. The checked examples separate immersion behavior from submersion behavior by injectivity versus surjectivity of the derivative.

A local diffeomorphism is where the derivative is invertible and the inverse actually behaves locally. The grid check uses a map with determinant one, reconstructs inverse values on a sample grid, and finds maximum residual at roundoff, so the inverse function theorem is computationally visible.

Immersion and embedding are deliberately separated here. A curve can have injective derivative without giving a topological embedding, and the dense torus trace makes that failure memorable. The cusp and figure-eight examples keep the smooth and topological failure modes distinct.

Submersions should feel like reliable projection devices. The circle level set is regular on sampled unit points because the gradient has rank one, while the crossed level set has a critical origin. The contrast explains why regular value hypotheses matter.

Covering maps add topology to the rank story. Local sections choose sheets that compose back to the identity on the base interval, and the sampled derivative norms stay nonzero. The interactive covering lab lets students see local triviality without pretending it is global injectivity.

Close with the applied lab because it tests the chapter's habit of watching rank under perturbation. The determinant three y squared minus a gives no rank-drop lines for negative a, one line at a equal zero, and two rank-drop lines for positive a.
